data.title: Staff Susceptible to Credential Phishing
data.summary: A simulated phishing campaign obtained credentials from staff, and in some cases a valid session, by presenting a convincing sign-in page from a look-alike domain. Credential phishing remains the most reliable route to initial access.
data.description:
Phishing works because it asks people to do something they do every day. The message resembles legitimate traffic, the sign-in page is a copy of the real one, and the request — reauthenticate, review a document, confirm a payment — is ordinary.

Modern kits operate as transparent proxies between the user and the real service. The victim authenticates genuinely, completes multi-factor authentication, and the kit captures the resulting session cookie. Push and one-time-code factors are therefore bypassed, which is why phishing-resistant factors bound to the origin are the control that matters.

Blaming users is both unfair and ineffective: the messages are designed to be indistinguishable, and a workforce that fears sanction reports less, which costs the defender the early warning that limits the damage.
data.recommendation:
* Deploy phishing-resistant MFA — FIDO2 or passkeys — for all staff, prioritising privileged and finance roles. This defeats proxy kits outright.
* Provide a one-click report button and respond visibly to every report, so reporting is rewarded.
* Measure the reporting rate and time-to-report, not only the click rate; the click is inevitable, the report is the control.
* Block look-alike domains, flag external mail clearly, and monitor certificate transparency for domains resembling yours.
* Run simulations as training with immediate, blame-free feedback, never as a disciplinary instrument.
data.short_recommendation: Deploy phishing-resistant MFA and make reporting easy.
